questions.q: What name does the chapter give to the Indus/Harappan/Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation in the story of India's cities?
questions.a: The chapter calls the Harappan civilisation India's 'First Urbanisation'.

questions.q: In which period did the new phase of city life called the Second Urbanisation begin?
questions.a: The Second Urbanisation began in the 1st millennium BCE; the early 2nd millennium BCE is when the Harappan cities disintegrated.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Historians can learn about the new cities of the Second Urbanisation from ancient texts.
Reason (R): Late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain literatures are full of references to these new urban centres.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: historians can learn about the new cities from ancient texts because late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain literatures refer again and again to these new urban centres.

questions.q:
Three imagined finds are dated by archaeologists. Read the statements about them.
Statement I: A small town in north India dated to about 1500 BCE belongs to the Second Urbanisation.
Statement II: A new walled city in the Indus basin dated to about 600 BCE could belong to the Second Urbanisation.
Statement III: A city in south India dated to about 300 BCE could belong to the Second Urbanisation.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. The Second Urbanisation began in the 1st millennium BCE in the Ganga plains, parts of the Indus basin and neighbouring regions, and spread gradually to other parts, with southern cities emerging from about 400 BCE. A town of about 1500 BCE falls in the millennium without urban life (Statement I), when there may only have been a few towns here and there in north India.

questions.q: (a) Name the two main sources from which we know about the Second Urbanisation. (b) Give one example of the ancient literature that refers to its new urban centres.
questions.a: (a) Archaeological excavations, which have confirmed the ancient urban centres, and ancient literature describing them. (b) Any one of late Vedic, Buddhist or Jain literature.
s: (a) Names both sources: archaeological excavations and ancient literature
(b) Gives one of late Vedic, Buddhist or Jain literature

questions.q: True or False? 'After the Harappan cities declined, some people went on living in a few of them, but in a rural or village way of life.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says some cities were abandoned, while in others some people continued living there but reverted to a rural or village lifestyle, because all the parts of the urban order had disappeared.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: in some cities people stayed on but reverted to village life, as the urban order (markets, administration, writing and so on) had disappeared

questions.q: The chapter lists what disappeared when the Harappan urban order ended. Explain in three short points what city life in the Harappan cities included, using three of these components.
questions.a: Any three of: elaborate private and public structures; crowded streets and busy markets; communities with specialised occupations such as metalsmiths, potters, builders and weavers; a writing system; a sanitation system; an administration; a larger state structure with a ruling class at the head.
s: First correct component from the chapter's list, for example busy markets
Second correct component, for example a writing system
Third correct component, for example an administration or a sanitation system

questions.q: A historian gathers three pieces of evidence about an old city in the Ganga plains: (i) a Buddhist text describing its busy market; (ii) the base of its fortification wall, uncovered by digging; (iii) a Jain text naming its streets. (a) Sort the three into the two kinds of sources the chapter names. (b) Which kind shows that the city really stood on the ground? (c) Why is it useful for the historian to have both kinds?
questions.a: (a) (i) and (iii) are ancient literature; (ii) is archaeological evidence from excavation. (b) The excavated wall: the chapter says excavations have confirmed the existence of the ancient urban centres. (c) The texts describe how the city lived (markets, streets), while the excavation confirms the place existed; together they give a fuller and more reliable picture.
s: (a) Sorts (i) and (iii) as ancient literature and (ii) as archaeological evidence
(b) Names the excavated wall, since excavations confirm the urban centres existed
(c) Explains that texts describe city life while digging confirms it, so both together give a fuller, more reliable picture

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A museum in Patna is planning a gallery called 'Two Urbanisations'. Room 1 will show the Harappan cities, which disintegrated in the early 2nd millennium BCE. Room 2 will show 'the thousand years in between'. Room 3 will show the new cities of the 1st millennium BCE in the Ganga plains, parts of the Indus basin and neighbouring regions. Four exhibits are still to be placed: a model of a covered drain from a planned street, the remains of a small farming village built over an abandoned city, a copy of a Buddhist text describing a busy new city, and a photograph of a crowded street in a present-day city that was a capital 2,500 years ago.
(a) In which rooms should the drain model and the farming-village remains go? Give a reason for each.
(b) In which room should the Buddhist text go, and why?
(c) The curator wants to label Room 2 'Nobody lived here'. Correct the label using the chapter.
(d) Does the photograph of the present-day street belong in this gallery? Use the chapter to decide.
questions.a: (a) The drain model goes in Room 1, because a sanitation system was part of the Harappan urban order; the farming-village remains go in Room 2, because people who stayed on reverted to a rural or village lifestyle. (b) Room 3: Buddhist literature is one of the texts full of references to the new urban centres of the Second Urbanisation. (c) People did live there: some continued living in old cities in a village way of life, there were important regional cultures, and there may even have been a few towns in north India; what was absent was urban life. (d) Yes, at the end of Room 3: the chapter says the Second Urbanisation has continued right up to today, and many ancient capitals are still living cities.
s: (a) Drain model in Room 1 (Harappan sanitation system); village remains in Room 2 (reversion to rural life)
(b) Buddhist text in Room 3, as Buddhist literature refers to the new urban centres
(c) Corrects the label: people still lived there in villages and regional cultures, possibly a few towns; only urban life was absent
(d) Decides yes, at the end of Room 3, because the Second Urbanisation has continued to today

questions.q:
Your class runs a stall called 'From Harappa to the Ganga' at the school fair. Answer each visitor in one line, using the chapter.
(a) A visitor reads that the Harappan cities disintegrated 'in the early 2nd millennium BCE'. What does this mean in years?
(b) The stall's banner says 'The Indus civilisation'. Give the two other names the chapter uses for it.
(c) A visitor asks how long urban life stayed absent from India after the Harappan cities. What do you tell her?
(d) A visitor says the new phase of cities began only in the Ganga plains. Correct him.
(e) A child asks why the new phase is called the 'Second' Urbanisation. Answer her.
questions.a: (a) Over a few centuries after 2000 BCE. (b) Harappan and Sindhu-Sarasvati. (c) For a whole millennium (about a thousand years), though there may have been a few towns here and there in north India. (d) It began in the Ganga plains, parts of the Indus (Sindhu) basin and neighbouring regions, and gradually spread to other parts of the Subcontinent. (e) Because the Harappan civilisation was India's 'First Urbanisation'; the new city life of the 1st millennium BCE was the next such phase.
s: (a) Over a few centuries after 2000 BCE
(b) Harappan and Sindhu-Sarasvati
(c) A whole millennium (about 1,000 years)
(d) Also parts of the Indus (Sindhu) basin and neighbouring regions
(e) The Harappan civilisation was the First Urbanisation, so this later phase is the Second

questions.q: What does the Sanskrit word 'janapada' mean?
o: Where the people have set foot, that is, have settled down
A large state formed when several kingdoms merged
An assembly of the elders of a clan
A fortified capital surrounded by a moat
questions.a: 'Janapada' means 'where the people (jana) have set foot (pada)', that is, where they have settled down.

questions.q:
Match each mahajanapada in Column A with its capital in Column B.
Column A: 1. Anga  2. Shurasena  3. Matsya  4. Avanti
Column B: a. Virata  b. Ujjayini  c. Champa  d. Mathura
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: Anga's capital was Champa, Shurasena's Mathura, Matsya's Virata and Avanti's Ujjayini.

questions.q:
Put these developments in the order the chapter describes them.
P: Clans come to be associated with a territory led by a raja.
Q: Some early states merge into bigger units called mahajanapadas.
R: Janapadas grow as trade networks expand and connect them.
S: The mahajanapadas cease to exist.
questions.a: P, R, Q, S: clans settle into janapadas, the janapadas grow as trade links them, by the 8th or 7th centuries BCE some merge into mahajanapadas, and by about 300 or 200 BCE the mahajanapadas cease to exist.

questions.q: (a) How many mahajanapadas are named in the more frequent list given in the texts? (b) Name the four that the chapter calls the most powerful of these new states.
questions.a: (a) 16 mahajanapadas. (b) Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti.
s: (a) States 16
(b) Names Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti

questions.q: A merchant of about 600 BCE starts at Champa, sells cloth at Rajagriha and ends his journey at Kaushambi. (a) Name the mahajanapada whose capital each of these three cities was, in order. (b) Which of the four states that the chapter calls the most powerful does his journey NOT reach?
questions.a: (a) Anga (Champa), Magadha (Rajagriha), Vatsa (Kaushambi). (b) Kosala and Avanti: the four most powerful were Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti, and he reaches only Magadha and Vatsa.
s: (a) Anga, Magadha, Vatsa in order
(b) Kosala and Avanti, after removing Magadha and Vatsa from the four most powerful

questions.q: A guide in today's Rajgir in Bihar tells visitors, 'You are walking in a city that was a capital about 2,500 years ago.' (a) Rajgir was once Rajagriha. Of which mahajanapada was it the capital? (b) What does the chapter say about most of the ancient capitals that supports the guide?
questions.a: (a) Magadha. (b) Most of those ancient capitals continue to be living cities today, 'modern' cities that are often 2,500 years old.
s: (a) Names Magadha
(b) States that most ancient capitals are still living cities, often 2,500 years old

questions.q: A student is drawing a mahajanapada capital for the class chart. Name three features she must show, and say in a few words what each one was for.
questions.a: (1) Strong fortifications or rampart walls round a large city, for defence. (2) A moat, a deep wide ditch filled with water, running outside the fortifications as further defence. (3) Narrow gateways through the rampart walls, so that guards could control the movement of people and goods entering or leaving the city.
s: Fortifications or rampart walls, for defence
A water-filled moat outside the walls, as further defence
Narrow gateways, so guards could control who and what entered or left

questions.q: A worksheet makes three claims. Claim 1: Ashmaka was a mahajanapada in central India, close to the Godavari River. Claim 2: Every one of the sixteen mahajanapadas lay in the Ganga plains. Claim 3: The chapter gives the growth of agriculture in the fertile Ganga plains as one possible reason why many mahajanapadas were found there. (a) Which two claims cannot both be true? Explain why. (b) Which of those two is wrong? (c) Rewrite it so that it matches the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Claims 1 and 2: Ashmaka lay near the Godavari in central India, outside the Ganga plains, so not every mahajanapada can have lain in the Ganga plains. Claim 3 fits with both. (b) Claim 2 is wrong; Claim 1 is what the chapter says (and Claim 3 is also correct). (c) 'Many of the mahajanapadas were concentrated in the Ganga plains, but not all; some, such as Ashmaka near the Godavari and Gandhara in the northwest, lay outside them.'
s: (a) Picks Claims 1 and 2 and explains that Ashmaka, near the Godavari, lay outside the Ganga plains
(b) Identifies Claim 2 as the wrong one
(c) Rewrites it: many of the mahajanapadas were in the Ganga plains, but not all

questions.q: Answer this task on the mahajanapadas. (a) Name the capital of Kosala. (b) Name the capital of Vatsa. (c) In parts of which present-day states did Kosala and Avanti lie, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) Shravasti. (b) Kaushambi. (c) Kosala lay in part of today's Uttar Pradesh and Avanti in part of today's Madhya Pradesh.
s: (a) Names Shravasti as the capital of Kosala
(b) Names Kaushambi as the capital of Vatsa
(c) Kosala in part of Uttar Pradesh and Avanti in part of Madhya Pradesh (1 mark each)

questions.q: At the start of the chapter Kautilya advises that a kingdom should fortify its capital, have cultivable land, have mines, and have good roads and a productive economy with many goods. Judge how well a mahajanapada of the Ganga plains could meet this advice. Match each of the four pieces of advice to evidence from the chapter, and then give your overall judgement.
questions.a: (1) Fortify the capital: most mahajanapada capitals were large, well-fortified cities with a moat and narrow gateways. (2) Cultivable land: the fertile Ganga plains allowed agriculture to grow. (3) Mines: iron ore was available in the mountains and hills. (4) Roads and a productive economy: new trade networks formed and connected the states. (5) Judgement: a Ganga-plains mahajanapada met Kautilya's advice well, which is one reason so many mahajanapadas were concentrated there.
s: Fortified capital matched to walls, moat and narrow gateways of the capitals
Cultivable land matched to the growth of agriculture in the fertile Ganga plains
Mines matched to iron ore in the mountains and hills
Roads and economy matched to the new trade networks
Overall judgement supported by the evidence (met it well, explaining the concentration in the Ganga plains)

questions.q: What was the assembly or council of a janapada, where matters concerning the clan were discussed, called?
questions.a: The assembly or council of a janapada was called the sabha or samiti.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The raja of a monarchy such as Magadha maintained an army.
Reason (R): The chapter says there was never any warfare between neighbouring mahajanapadas.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the king maintained an army to defend the territory or wage war with neighbouring ones, and the chapter says there is some evidence of warfare between neighbouring mahajanapadas, though how frequent it was is impossible to tell.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement I: In their political systems, the mahajanapadas expanded the basic principles of the janapadas.
Statement II: Scholars call Vajji and Malla 'early republics' because they are one of the earliest such systems in the world.
Statement III: In the monarchies, the raja ruled without any ministers or assembly of elders.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. The mahajanapadas expanded the basic principles of the janapadas (I), and scholars have called Vajji and Malla 'early republics', one of the earliest such systems in the world (II). Statement III is wrong: in the monarchies the raja was the ultimate authority but was supported by ministers and an assembly of elders.

questions.q: True or False? 'The only duty of a raja in a monarchy such as Magadha was to fight wars with neighbouring states.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The king collected taxes or revenue, maintained law and order, got impressive fortifications built around the capital, and maintained an army to defend the territory or wage war with neighbours, as the case may be.
s: States the verdict: False
Reason: he also collected taxes, kept law and order and built fortifications; even the army was to defend the territory as well as to wage war

questions.q: In a mahajanapada, a band of raiders keeps attacking traders near the capital, and the raja's treasury is almost empty. (a) Which duty of the king named in the chapter deals with the raiders? (b) Which duty deals with the empty treasury?
questions.a: (a) Maintaining law and order, and keeping an army to defend the territory. (b) Collecting taxes or revenue.
s: (a) Links the raiders to maintaining law and order / maintaining an army
(b) Links the empty treasury to collecting taxes or revenue

questions.q: Answer in one line each about Vajji and Malla. (a) What were such mahajanapadas called? (b) How did their sabha or samiti take important decisions? (c) What name have scholars often given them?
questions.a: (a) Ganas or sanghas. (b) Through discussion and, if necessary, through a vote. (c) 'Early republics', one of the earliest such systems in the world.
s: (a) Ganas or sanghas
(b) Through discussion and, if necessary, a vote
(c) Early republics

questions.q: Compare Avanti and Vajji on three powers: (i) choosing the raja, (ii) giving advice, (iii) taking the important decisions. For each power, say who held it in Avanti and who held it in Vajji.
questions.a: (i) Choosing the raja: in Avanti nobody chose him, as the post was hereditary (usually the son of the previous raja); in Vajji the assembly selected the raja. (ii) Giving advice: in Avanti ministers and an assembly of elders advised the raja; in Vajji the assembly discussed matters itself. (iii) Important decisions: in Avanti the raja was the ultimate authority; in Vajji the sabha or samiti took the important decisions through discussion and, if necessary, a vote.
s: (i) Avanti hereditary succession vs Vajji assembly selects the raja
(ii) Avanti ministers and elders advise the raja vs Vajji assembly discusses matters itself
(iii) Avanti raja is ultimate authority vs Vajji assembly decides by discussion and vote

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Ratnapura is an invented monarchy of about 550 BCE. In one year its raja (1) collected a share of grain and silver as revenue from 1,200 farming families; (2) had the rampart round his capital rebuilt, with a deeper water-filled ditch outside it and narrower gateways; (3) posted 300 soldiers on the border after a neighbouring state threatened it; (4) appointed guards and judges to settle quarrels in the markets. He listens to his ministers and an assembly of elders, but the final word is always his.
(a) Name the duty of the king, as the chapter lists it, behind actions (1), (3) and (4).
(b) Give the chapter's reason for the deeper ditch and for the narrower gateways in action (2).
(c) What makes Ratnapura a monarchy in the chapter's sense, even though the raja listens to an assembly?
(d) Which piece of Kautilya's advice at the start of the chapter does action (2) follow?
questions.a: (a) (1) Collecting taxes or revenue; (3) maintaining an army to defend the territory; (4) maintaining law and order. (b) The moat, a deep wide ditch filled with water, runs outside the fortifications as further defence; the gateways are kept narrow so that guards can control the movement of people and goods entering or leaving the city. (c) The raja is the ultimate authority; ministers and an assembly of elders only support him. (d) The kingdom should be protected by fortifying the capital (and the towns at the frontiers).
s: (a) Taxes or revenue for (1), an army for (3), law and order for (4)
(b) Moat as further defence; narrow gateways so guards control movement of people and goods
(c) The raja is the ultimate authority, supported by ministers and elders
(d) Kautilya's advice to fortify the capital

questions.q: A speaker at a school debate says: 'Democratic ways of deciding were unknown in India until modern times.' Test this claim against the chapter. (a) Give one piece of evidence from the janapadas. (b) Give one piece of evidence from Vajji and Malla. (c) What have scholars called states like Vajji and Malla, and why? (d) Decide whether the claim stands, and add one caution the chapter itself gives about how far this evidence goes.
questions.a: (a) Each janapada had an assembly, the sabha or samiti, where clan matters were discussed, and the raja was not expected to rule independently or arbitrarily but to take its advice. (b) In Vajji and Malla the sabha or samiti took important decisions through discussion and, if necessary, a vote, and even selected the raja, so their functioning might be called democratic. (c) 'Early republics', as they are one of the earliest such systems in the world. (d) The claim does not stand: democratic traditions existed in some states in the 1st millennium BCE. Caution: only at least two mahajanapadas worked this way, while others such as Magadha, Kosala and Avanti were monarchies; and the data we have for such remote periods is incomplete.
s: (a) Janapada sabha or samiti, with the raja expected to take its advice
(b) Vajji and Malla decided by discussion and vote, even selecting the raja
(c) Early republics, one of the earliest such systems in the world
(d) Rejects the claim and adds a caution: only some states, others monarchies, or incomplete data

questions.q: A website says: 'The janapadas had a fixed law that the assembly must remove every bad ruler, so the raja was only a servant of the assembly.' Test this claim against the chapter. (a) What was the janapada assembly called, and where do these words first appear? (b) Who were most of its members likely to be? (c) What was a good ruler expected to do? (d) What do some texts say about an incompetent ruler, and why does the chapter refuse to call it an established law? (e) Decide: which part of the website's claim can be kept, and how must the rest be rewritten?
questions.a: (a) The sabha or samiti; the words first appear in the Vedas, India's most ancient texts. (b) We may assume most members were elders in the clan. (c) The raja was not expected to rule independently or arbitrarily; a good ruler was supposed to take advice from the assemblies, apart from ministers and administrators. (d) According to some texts an incompetent ruler could be removed by the assembly, but the chapter says this does not mean it was an established law, because the data for such remote periods is incomplete. (e) Keep only the idea that the assembly mattered and the raja was expected to take its advice; rewrite the rest: 'Some texts say an assembly could remove an incompetent ruler, but we cannot call this a fixed law; the raja led the janapada, taking counsel from the assembly.'
s: (a) Sabha or samiti, words first found in the Vedas
(b) Mostly elders of the clan
(c) Ruler not to rule arbitrarily; a good ruler took the assembly's advice, besides ministers and administrators
(d) Some texts say an incompetent ruler could be removed, but not an established law as the data is incomplete
(e) Decision: keeps the assembly's advisory importance, rejects 'fixed law' and 'servant', with a corrected statement

questions.q: Of which metal were the first Indian coins made?
questions.a: The first Indian coins were made of silver; coins of copper, gold and other metals came later.

questions.q:
Each situation in Column A comes from the age of the mahajanapadas. Match it with the development in Column B that best explains it.
Column A: 1. Villages now grow far more grain than in earlier times.  2. One state defeats its neighbour and a bigger kingdom is formed.  3. A merchant of Avanti is paid in coins made far away.  4. A Jain teaching from the Ganga plains reaches a distant city.
Column B: a. warfare and military campaigns  b. iron tools becoming widespread  c. scholars, monks and nuns travelling across India  d. coins being exchanged across regions in growing trade
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c: widespread iron tools made agriculture possible on a bigger scale; military campaigns gave rise to new kingdoms; coins were soon exchanged across different regions as trade grew; and the new schools of thought spread through scholars, monks and nuns travelling across India.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Symbols could be punched into the first Indian coins.
Reason (R): These coins were made of silver, a soft metal.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: silver is soft, so symbols could be punched into it, which is why they are called punch-marked coins.

questions.q: Which metals had the Harappan civilisation already mastered, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The Harappan civilisation mastered copper and bronze metallurgy; iron became central only in the Second Urbanisation.

questions.q: (a) From when were the techniques of extracting and shaping iron perfected in several regions of India? (b) By when had iron tools become widespread?
questions.a: (a) From the early 2nd millennium BCE. (b) By the late 2nd millennium BCE.
s: (a) Early 2nd millennium BCE
(b) Late 2nd millennium BCE

questions.q: True or False? 'There is evidence of warfare between neighbouring mahajanapadas, so we know that they fought all the time and never made alliances.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. There is some evidence of warfare, but the chapter says how frequent or how intense it was is impossible to tell; and occasionally alliances, as well as military campaigns, gave rise to new kingdoms and empires.
s: States the verdict: False
Correction: how often or how fiercely they fought cannot be told, and alliances too sometimes gave rise to new kingdoms

questions.q: Compare the First Urbanisation (Harappan) and the Second Urbanisation on three points, using the chapter: (a) the main metal technology, (b) the use of coins, (c) where the cities grew.
questions.a: (a) The Harappans mastered copper and bronze; the Second Urbanisation shifted to iron metallurgy. (b) Coins were first used in India in the Second Urbanisation, made necessary by growing trade, so the Harappan cities had none. (c) The Harappan cities were in the Indus/Sindhu-Sarasvati region; the new cities grew in the Ganga plains, parts of the Indus basin and neighbouring regions, then spread further.
s: (a) Copper and bronze for the Harappans vs iron in the Second Urbanisation
(b) First coins in India came only in the Second Urbanisation, due to growing trade
(c) Indus/Sindhu-Sarasvati region vs Ganga plains, parts of the Indus basin and beyond

questions.q: A trader in a mahajanapada city records 40 sales in one month: 22 were paid in coins of his own mahajanapada, 10 in coins issued by neighbouring regions, and 8 by exchanging goods without coins. He is thinking of refusing coins from neighbouring regions. (a) What percentage of the 40 sales were paid in coins? (b) What percentage of his sales would he risk losing if he refused neighbouring coins? (c) Using the chapter, decide whether he should refuse them.
questions.a: (a) 22 + 10 = 32 coin sales; 32 out of 40 = 80%. (b) 10 out of 40 = 25% of his sales. (c) He should not refuse them: the chapter says that although a mahajanapada generally issued its own coins, coins from neighbouring regions were used as well as exchanged in trade, and trade was growing; refusing them would put a quarter of his sales at risk.
s: (c) Decides not to refuse: neighbouring coins were normally used and exchanged in trade, and he would risk a quarter of his sales

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a village of the Ganga plains around 500 BCE, a smith heats a dark grey metal in a hot fire and beats it into ploughshares and sickles for the farmers. Farmers who use his tools are clearing and ploughing far more land than their grandparents did. At the village market a traveller pays for grain with coins; some are of silver, and the traveller says that in later times coins of other metals will be made too. One of his coins was made in a faraway region.
(a) Which metal is the smith working?
(b) How did tools of this metal help the farmers?
(c) Name two other metals of which coins were later made.
(d) What does the coin from a faraway region show about coins in this age?
questions.a: (a) Iron. (b) Iron tools became widespread and helped agriculture on a bigger scale. (c) Copper and gold. (d) Very soon after coins came into use, they were exchanged across different regions and even with other parts of the world.
s: (a) Iron
(b) Iron tools helped agriculture on a bigger scale
(c) Copper and gold
(d) Coins were exchanged across different regions and even with other parts of the world

questions.q: A student writes: 'Iron alone explains why cities grew again in India in the 1st millennium BCE.' Evaluate the claim. (a) Give one way in which iron did help, according to the chapter. (b) Use the chapter's dates to show that knowing how to work iron did not by itself bring back city life. (c) Name one development linked to trade that the chapter connects with the growth of the new states. (d) Name one reason, other than iron ore, that the chapter offers for so many mahajanapadas lying in the Ganga plains. (e) Give your verdict on the claim.
questions.a: (a) By the late 2nd millennium BCE iron tools had become widespread, facilitating agriculture on a bigger scale (iron also made lighter, sharper weapons). (b) Iron techniques were perfected in several regions from the early 2nd millennium BCE, the very period in which the Harappan cities disintegrated, yet urban life stayed absent for a whole millennium; so the knowledge of iron existed for centuries without cities. (c) The janapadas grew as trade networks expanded and connected them, and growing trade made coins necessary. (d) The growth of agriculture in the fertile Ganga plains, or the formation of new trade networks. (e) The claim is too strong: iron was a major shift in technology, but the new cities grew from iron together with fertile land, expanding trade networks and coins.
s: (a) Iron tools widespread by the late 2nd millennium BCE, helping agriculture on a bigger scale
(b) Iron techniques from the early 2nd millennium BCE, yet a whole millennium without urban life
(c) Trade networks connecting the janapadas, or coins made necessary by trade
(d) Fertile Ganga plains agriculture or new trade networks
(e) Verdict: claim too strong; iron worked together with land, trade and coins

questions.q: According to the chapter, during which period, in particular, did the varna-jati system become more rigid?
o: During the British rule in India
During the age of the Harappan cities
During the age of the janapadas
During the rise of the first coins
questions.a: The chapter says the system became more rigid with the passage of time, in particular during the British rule in India.

questions.q:
Match each varna in Column A with its role in Column B.
Column A: 1. Brahmins  2. Kshatriyas  3. Vaishyas  4. Shudras
Column B: a. increase the society's wealth through trade, business or agriculture  b. artisans, craftspeople, workers or servants  c. preserve and spread knowledge and perform rituals  d. defend the society and the land
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: Brahmins preserved and spread knowledge and performed rituals, Kshatriyas defended the society and land, Vaishyas increased wealth through trade, business or agriculture, and Shudras were artisans, craftspeople, workers or servants.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement I: A family of potters whose skill passes from parents to children over generations is an example of a jati, a community defined by its occupation.
Statement II: In the early period, a Brahmin who took up trade was doing something the chapter says never happened.
Statement III: The chapter says the varna-jati system brought only inequality and never gave society any stability.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I only. A jati is a community with a specific occupation whose defining skill was generally passed from generation to generation, so the potter family is an example of one (I). Statement II is wrong: there is evidence that some Brahmins turned to trade or even military activities. Statement III is wrong: the system organised society's activities and gave it some stability, though in time it became rigid and led to inequalities.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): As a society grows more complex, it organises itself into several groups based on class, occupation or other criteria.
Reason (R): Equality is an ideal that very few human societies, if any, have ever achieved.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: societies form groups because they grow more complex, while R is about the inequalities that such divisions often lead to.

questions.q: (a) What is a jati? (b) Give one example of a skill that could define a jati.
questions.a: (a) A jati is a group or community of people with a specific professional occupation closely tied to their livelihood, whose skills were generally passed from generation to generation. (b) Any one of skill in agriculture, metallurgy, commerce or a craft.
s: (a) Defines a jati as a community with a specific occupation tied to livelihood, skills passed down generations
(b) Gives one skill: agriculture, metallurgy, commerce or a craft

questions.q: True or False? 'A jati could be divided further into sub-jatis, each with customs and traditions of its own, for example about marriage or food habits.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says a jati would often get further subdivided into sub-jatis, each of which developed its own customs and traditions, for instance concerning marriage, rituals or food habits.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: jatis were often subdivided into sub-jatis with their own customs on marriage, rituals or food habits

questions.q: The chapter says Indian society was organised in a 'two-fold system'. (a) Name the two categories of this system. (b) Which category was based on a specific occupation tied to livelihood? (c) Which category emerged from the Vedic texts, and how many groups did it have?
questions.a: (a) Jati and varna. (b) Jati. (c) Varna, which had four groups: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras.
s: (a) Names jati and varna
(b) Jati
(c) Varna, with four groups

questions.q: Explain what each situation shows about the varna-jati system as the chapter describes it. (i) A family of metalsmiths has worked iron for four generations, each parent teaching the children the craft. (ii) In the early period, a family of potters becomes a family of traders when circumstances change. (iii) In a town, farmers, smiths, traders and priests each know their own work, so the fields, workshops and markets run smoothly.
questions.a: (i) It shows a jati: the skill that defines it, here metallurgy, is passed from generation to generation. (ii) It shows that the early system was flexible: individuals and communities changed their occupations if circumstances demanded. (iii) It shows that the system structured society and organised its activities, including economic ones, and so gave it some stability.
s: (i) A jati, with skills passed down generations
(ii) Flexibility of the early system: occupations changed when circumstances demanded
(iii) The system organised society's activities, including economic ones, giving it some stability

questions.q: A student keeps mixing up jati and varna. Write a clear comparison for her under four headings: (a) what the group is based on, (b) where the idea comes from or how it is passed on, (c) how many groups there are, (d) whether it can be divided further.
questions.a: (a) Jati is based on a specific professional occupation tied to livelihood; varna is a broad grouping by role in society (knowledge and rituals, defence, wealth, crafts and service). (b) Jati skills were passed from generation to generation; varna is a concept that emerged from the Vedic texts. (c) The chapter names four varnas; it gives no number for the jatis. (d) A jati could be subdivided into sub-jatis with their own customs; the chapter names four varnas and describes no division of them.
s: (a) Jati by specific occupation vs varna by broad role in society
(b) Jati skills passed down generations vs varna from Vedic texts
(c) Four varnas; no number given for jatis
(d) Jatis subdivided into sub-jatis vs the chapter describing no division of the four varnas

questions.q:
Correct each of these five sentences from a student's notes in one line, using the chapter.
(a) 'There were five varnas.'
(b) 'The word caste comes from Sanskrit.'
(c) 'All scholars agree that the word caste means the four varnas.'
(d) 'Shudras were expected to defend the land.'
(e) 'The varna-jati system was rigid from the very beginning.'
questions.a: (a) There were four varnas. (b) 'Caste' comes from the Portuguese word casta, used by Portuguese travellers in the 16th century CE. (c) Only a few scholars take 'caste' to mean varnas; most take it to apply to jatis, and others to the whole varna-jati system. (d) Kshatriyas were expected to defend the land; Shudras were artisans, craftspeople, workers or servants. (e) The system was more flexible in earlier periods and became rigid with time.
s: (a) Four varnas
(b) From the Portuguese word casta
(c) A few scholars say varnas, most say jatis, others the whole system
(d) Kshatriyas defended the land; Shudras were artisans, workers or servants
(e) More flexible earlier, rigid later

questions.q: Which route connected the northwest regions to the Ganga plains, all the way to eastern India?
o: A lateral road to the western coast
A sea route to Southeast Asia
questions.a: The Uttarapatha connected the northwest regions to the Ganga plains, all the way to eastern India.

questions.q: A monk from the northwest walks along a great route through the Ganga plains to Kaushambi, then crosses the Vindhya Range and keeps going south to teach. Which routes has he used, in order?
o: The Uttarapatha, then a lateral road to the western coast
questions.a: The Uttarapatha, then the Dakshinapatha: the Uttarapatha connected the northwest regions to the Ganga plains, and the Dakshinapatha started from Kaushambi and crossed the Vindhya Range to go all the way south.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The new cities of the 1st millennium BCE grew only in the Ganga plains.
Reason (R): Sisupalgarh, capital of the Kalinga region in the east, followed a strict square ground plan with imposing fortifications and broad streets.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true: Sisupalgarh, a major city with a square plan, fortifications and broad streets, grew in the Kalinga region of the east, which itself shows that the new cities were not limited to the Ganga plains.

questions.q: (a) Name the two routes that became widely used in the 1st millennium BCE and are often mentioned in the literature. (b) Give two purposes for which such communication routes opened up.
questions.a: (a) The Uttarapatha and the Dakshinapatha. (b) Any two of trade, pilgrimage and military campaigns.
s: (a) Names the Uttarapatha and the Dakshinapatha
(b) Gives two of trade, pilgrimage, military campaigns

questions.q: True or False? 'By about 300 or 200 BCE the mahajanapadas had ceased to exist, so the links between the regions of the Subcontinent must have broken down.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. At about the same time as the mahajanapadas ceased to exist, almost the entire Subcontinent, including regions in the Northeast, was one vibrant interconnected land; goods and culture travelled from region to region and often beyond India.
s: States the verdict: False
Reason: at that very time the Subcontinent, including the Northeast, was one interconnected land with goods and culture moving between regions

questions.q: Answer in one line each about Sisupalgarh. (a) Of which region was it the capital? (b) Where does it lie today? (c) Name two features of its layout given in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Kalinga region. (b) It is today Sisupalgarh, part (a suburb) of Bhubaneswar. (c) Any two of: a strict square ground plan, imposing fortifications, broad streets (also a moat and narrow gateways, Fig. 4.7).
s: (a) Kalinga
(b) Part of / a suburb of Bhubaneswar
(c) Two layout features such as a strict square plan, imposing fortifications, broad streets

questions.q: Compare the Uttarapatha and the Dakshinapatha on three points: (a) where each began or what it connected, (b) the direction each ran, (c) one thing the two routes had in common.
questions.a: (a) The Uttarapatha connected the northwest regions to the Ganga plains; the Dakshinapatha started from Kaushambi (near Prayagraj), a capital of one of the mahajanapadas. (b) The Uttarapatha ran from the northwest east through the Ganga plains to eastern India; the Dakshinapatha ran south, crossing the Vindhya Range. (c) Both were widely used routes mentioned in literature, used for trade, pilgrimage and military campaigns.
s: (a) Uttarapatha links the northwest to the Ganga plains; Dakshinapatha starts at Kaushambi
(b) Uttarapatha runs west to east; Dakshinapatha runs south across the Vindhyas
(c) Common point: both widely used and mentioned in literature, for trade, pilgrimage, campaigns

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Around 250 BCE a merchant from the southern regions of the Subcontinent loads 50 bags onto a ship: 20 bags of spices, 18 bags of semiprecious stones and 12 bags of cotton cloth. His goods are sold in other parts of India and to buyers overseas. A visitor tells him, 'Your land had no cities or trade at all before 400 BCE.' The merchant replies that the kings of his land are even named in old poems in his own language.
(a) Which of the merchant's goods are among the resources the chapter says the southern regions were rich in? What percentage of his 50 bags do they make up?
(b) Why could the southern regions trade profitably beyond India?
(c) How does the chapter partly challenge the visitor's claim?
(d) Name the three kingdoms that emerged in the south around this time, and the literature that mentions them.
questions.a: (a) Spices and semiprecious stones: 20 + 18 = 38 of 50 bags = 76%. (b) The southern regions were rich in precious and semiprecious stones, gold and spices, so they traded profitably not only with the rest of India but with kingdoms and empires overseas. (c) Cities began emerging from about 400 BCE, but recent excavations claim to find signs of commercial activities going further back. (d) The Cholas, the Cheras and the Pandyas; the most ancient Tamil literature mentions them and several of their kings.
s: (a) Identifies spices and semiprecious stones and computes 38/50 = 76%
(b) Rich in precious and semiprecious stones, gold and spices, so they traded with India and overseas
(c) Recent excavations claim signs of commercial activity before 400 BCE
(d) Cholas, Cheras, Pandyas, mentioned in the most ancient Tamil literature

questions.q: A student claims: 'In the 1st millennium BCE the new roads mattered only to traders carrying goods.' Evaluate this claim. Give three pieces of evidence from the chapter that test it, and then state whether you accept or reject the claim.
questions.a: Evidence 1: The routes opened up for pilgrimage and military campaigns as well as trade. Evidence 2: The new schools of thought (late Vedic, Buddhist, Jain) spread through scholars, monks and nuns travelling across India and through pilgrimages. Evidence 3: The chapter's summary says people, goods, ideas and teachings travelled along all those roads. Judgement: reject the claim; roads mattered to traders, but also to pilgrims, armies, scholars and monks, and they carried ideas as well as goods.
s: Evidence: routes also served pilgrimage and military campaigns
Evidence: scholars, monks and nuns travelled to spread new schools of thought
Evidence: people, goods, ideas and teachings all travelled the roads
Judgement: rejects the claim, supported by the evidence

questions.q:
Your class wall-magazine is planning a page called 'One interconnected land, 300-200 BCE'. It has space for only three of these five pictures, and the three together must show the south, the east, and links beyond India.
P: The remains of a fortified city in the far south, built about 350 BCE.
Q: A busy port on the eastern coast, joined to the interior by roads.
R: Southern spices and gold being shipped to kingdoms overseas.
S: A Harappan city with its sanitation system.
T: A caption reading 'The sixteen mahajanapadas at the height of their power, 200 BCE'.
(a) What does P show about the south? (b) What does Q show about the east? (c) Why does R show links beyond India? (d) Give a reason for rejecting S and a reason for rejecting T. (e) State the three pictures chosen.
questions.a: (a) Cities began emerging in the Subcontinent's southern regions from about 400 BCE, so a southern city of about 350 BCE shows the south had joined the urban world. (b) Many lateral roads connected other parts of India with the important ports on the eastern and western coasts, which were vibrant centres of trade. (c) The southern regions, rich in precious and semiprecious stones, gold and spices, traded profitably not only with the rest of India but with kingdoms and empires overseas. (d) S belongs to the First Urbanisation, which disintegrated in the early 2nd millennium BCE, long before this period; T is wrong, because about this time the mahajanapadas ceased to exist. (e) P, Q and R.
s: (a) P: southern cities emerged from about 400 BCE
(b) Q: lateral roads linked the interior to vibrant ports on the eastern coast
(c) R: the south's stones, gold and spices were traded with kingdoms and empires overseas
(d) Rejects S (Harappan, First Urbanisation, much earlier) and T (mahajanapadas ceased about then)
(e) Chooses P, Q and R
